accepted_lineage.note: First draft of S1 from C03, following B01. B01 risks handled: requirements are defined by asking what the sea did first (open water with the sea behind versus a shingle bank), the hull is an existing 24 m flat hull from the Orsay contract with a trunked lifting board (modular path), the pivot and frames are cross-checked by each yard in the other's units and then in millimetres, the shear pin is the apprentice's idea, and the boat is tested first on the bank (board housed, then board half down so the pin shears) and then in the Sound by an independent surveyor with explicit abort thresholds. story.title: THE LIFEBOAT TWO YARDS BUILT
story.deck: A surge is nine days off and the condemned ferry cannot sail. Two boatyards that have not shared a slip in thirty years each remember a drowning the other's boat would repeat; Illuminara asks them what the sea did first.
story.shape: Seven scenes across nine days: an argument on the shingle, a day in each yard, a chalk floor where one number turns out to be two, a night spent holding a hull still, a trial in two seas, and three crossings with one family choosing to stay.

scenes.title: The Argument on the Shingle
paragraphs: *Skerrow, Tolland Slip · nine days before the surge, 06:40*

The ferry lay where the tide had left her, plating opened along one side like a tin. The surveyor's notice on her wheelhouse door was three days old. The forecast was newer: a surge in nine days, high water at 21:40, and a sea that would walk over the quay and into the lower village. Three hundred and ten people lived on Skerrow. The coastguard cutter could carry forty, if the sea allowed, and nobody would promise the sea.

Illuminara had come over on a fishing boat with a flask and a notebook. The council clerk had asked for hands that could hold a hull still while it was joined. Nobody had asked her for a design, and she was beginning to see why.
Two people had reached the slip from opposite ends of the shingle, and neither had slowed down.

**Magnus**  
There is a hull in my shed from the Orsay contract. Twenty-four metres, flat as a table, and she takes a bank like a hand takes a glove. I can have her on the slip by noon.

**Adaeze**  
And in the first following sea off the Sound she lies down. Flat doesn't grip. My brother learned that in the time it takes to say it. I won't send three hundred people out on a tray.

**Magnus**  
And your deep keel stands off Pellam Bank with nowhere to put its nose, and breaks up in the surf. My father learned that. Look at the stones.
Nobody looked at the stones. They looked at each other, the way people look at a wall they helped to build.

**Illuminara**  
I can hold a hull level while it is joined, and carry a load through it for a while. I can't draw a keel, and I can't draw a bank. Is each of you right about the other's boat?

**Adaeze**  
Yes.

**Magnus**  
Yes.

**Illuminara**  
Then I would like a day in each yard. Not to choose between you. To be corrected.
Magnus laughed first, short and unwilling. It was the first sound the two of them had made together in thirty years, and neither forgave the other for it.

scenes.title: The Loft
paragraphs: *Oyelaran yard, mould loft · nine days before the surge, 15:10*

Chalk lines covered the loft floor, every offset marked in Adaeze's fractions of a foot. A seventeen-year-old called Tobi had been told to teach the visitor to plane a keel timber and had decided to do it thoroughly.

**Tobi**  
Thumb forward. No, you're pushing the wood. The plane does the pushing. There. Hear that? That's a shaving, not a splinter.

Illuminara had stood inside a great many collapsing things and had never heard this sound. The oak smelled like a held breath. *I am being taught by a boy with sawdust in his eyebrows,* she thought, *and I am happier than I have been all week.*
Adaeze came up the stairs with two mugs and did not sit.

**Adaeze**  
Kehinde's boat was flat. A good boat, fast. Running home with the sea behind her, the stern came up on a wave and the bow dug, and for half a second she had nothing under her to hold the water. Then she swung beam-on, and the next wave finished it.

**Illuminara**  
What did the sea do first?

**Adaeze**  
The stern lifted. Everyone asks how big the wave was. You're the first to ask what it did first.
Illuminara wrote *stern lifts, no grip, swings beam-on* in her notebook, and under it, *open water, sea behind.* Adaeze watched her write it the way one watches a stranger handle a tool one has made.

**Adaeze**  
A keel is not a theory. It's the part of the boat that remembers the water.

scenes.title: The Bank
paragraphs: *Fenn yard, ramp and shingle · eight days before the surge, 07:20*

Wick, sixteen, put a chain in her hands and moved her grip before she had closed them. Everything on the Fenn ramp was measured in the yard's own rule, tenths of a foot, in pencil on the planking. Magnus walked the shingle beside her and told it to the stones rather than to her.

**Magnus**  
My father's boat had a good deep keel. Fine in the Sound. At Harbour Tarn there was no quay, only a bank like Pellam. He brought her in to ground her, and the keel took the shingle and stopped her dead while the surf kept coming. She lay down forty yards from dry stones.

**Illuminara**  
What did the sea do first?
He looked at her as if she had been impertinent. Then he answered.

**Magnus**  
The keel stopped. First. Then she turned over.

That night, on a sheet of the yard's brown paper, Illuminara wrote the two answers side by side. Adaeze's brother had died in open water, with the sea behind him and nothing to grip. Magnus's father had died on a bank, with the sea on the beam and too much to grip. *Two boats,* she thought. *Two different minutes of the same crossing.* Nobody had ever asked one hull to survive both.

scenes.title: Seven in Two Languages
paragraphs: *The old sail loft · seven days before the surge, 21:30*

Lamplight, and the two masters on opposite sides of it. Tobi and Wick stood against the wall with the look of apprentices who expect to be sent out. Illuminara had chalked two columns on the floor, every figure converted into millimetres. In one: OPEN WATER, SEA BEHIND. Needs grip along the length. In the other: THE BANK. Needs a flat bottom and nothing that can dig.

On the table lay a third sheet, brown at the folds, found at the bottom of the island's drawing chest. The Marigold, the one boat the two yards had ever drawn together, thirty years ago. Her keel was drawn at seven.

**Illuminara**  
Both your hands are on this sheet. What does seven mean?

**Adaeze**  
Seven-eighths of a foot.

**Magnus**  
Seven-tenths. It's what seven has always meant.

Seven-eighths of a foot is two hundred and sixty-seven millimetres. Seven-tenths is two hundred and thirteen. The Marigold had been built fifty-four millimetres too shallow, and she had rolled on her moorings the night she was launched, and for thirty years each yard had known exactly whose fault that was.
Nobody said sorry. Adaeze took the chalk and wrote 267 beside the seven. Magnus, after a long moment, took it from her and wrote 213 beneath it, and the two of them stood looking at the difference.

**Illuminara**  
Both are good drawings. You were reading one number in two languages.

**Magnus**  
Then show me a boat that does both, and I'll stop saying it can't be built.

**Adaeze**  
A board through the bottom. Down in the Sound, with the sea behind her, it gives her something to hold.

**Magnus**  
A hole in the bottom of a boat. That is near enough how my father went.

**Adaeze**  
A trunk to deck height. The hole is above the water.

**Magnus**  
And on the bank the board is down and she stops dead, the way he did.

**Tobi**  
Raise it before she lands. And if she meets shingle with the board half down it should kick up, not dig. A pin that shears. A winch to haul it, and a crank for when the winch won't.
Nobody answered an apprentice for a while. Adaeze looked at Magnus. Magnus looked at Wick, who looked at the floor, and then, with some effort, at Tobi.

**Magnus**  
Who owns what?

**Adaeze**  
Board, trunk and pivot are mine. Hull, ramp and the framing around my slot are yours.

**Magnus**  
I check your pivot load in your units.

**Adaeze**  
And I check your frames in yours. Then we both do it again in millimetres and sign each other's sheets.

**Illuminara**  
I'll hold her still while you cut.

scenes.title: Standing Still
paragraphs: *Tolland Slip, shed two · four days before the surge, 02:10*

Four days had gone into the hull and the trunk. The two yards worked in alternating shifts so that neither slept while the other's hands were on the boat. Now she sat on her blocks with a seam of lamplight where the slot would go. Fourteen tonnes of plating wanted to spring the moment Tobi's saw finished the first cut; a flat hull opens badly.

Illuminara laid both palms against the plating beside the line and took the load through herself, down her arms and her spine into the slip, the way one holds a door against wind. The plating stayed true. For fifty minutes Magnus cut and Tobi cut and Adaeze measured, and she did not move.

It cost her. Her hands shook long before the slot was done, and when Magnus said, without looking up, that she might let go, she sat down on an upturned bucket and could not lift a mug. Tobi brought her tea and, with a straight face, a plane.

**Tobi**  
Your grip is still wrong.
*Good,* she thought, and was surprised again by how much she meant it.

scenes.title: Two Seas
paragraphs: *Pellam Bank and Skerrow Sound · two days before the surge, 08:00*

She went down the slip at first light, ugly, with the trunk running down her middle like a spine. The surveyor, Hanne Voss, was sixty and had refused certificates for far prettier boats. She read her conditions aloud before anyone touched the engine.

**Hanne**  
Abort thresholds first. Heel past fifteen degrees and holding, I call her in. A board that doesn't answer a command inside twenty seconds, I call her in. Water at the trunk lid, I call her in. Sea above three metres significant, I call her in. I will not be argued with, by either yard or by you.

At Pellam Bank, on the rising tide, the boat ran at the shingle at five knots with the board housed and a hundred and forty barrels of ballast aboard. Her flat bottom rode up the bank and stopped without a shudder. Then, on Hanne's order, they did it again with the board dropped halfway. It struck, the pin sheared, and the board swung up into its trunk like a hand taken off a hot stove. Tobi drew the stub and fitted a fresh pin in four minutes. Magnus watched the whole of it with his arms folded.

**Magnus**  
Good pin.
In his mouth it was a speech.

In the Sound that afternoon the swell ran two and a half metres from astern. The boat lifted her stern on the first wave with the board down, and she did not swing. Adaeze stood at the rail with one hand flat on her chest and did not speak until the third wave had passed. Hanne wrote on her board, and wrote again.

**Hanne**  
A hundred and forty seats on my certificate. Three hundred and ten islanders. Two full crossings and a short third, each a little under six hours round trip. The sea builds through the last day. If the third has to wait for a window, it waits, and the cutter takes forty before it.

scenes.title: Three Crossings
paragraphs: *Tolland Slip to Pellam Bank · the day before the surge, 06:30*

Ruth Calloway's family did not come to the slip. Illuminara went up the hill instead and found Ruth on her step with a flask. Five of them lived in that house, and the church where her mother lay was thirty-four metres above the sea.

**Ruth**  
I've lived through eleven forecasts. We are staying.

**Illuminara**  
What would make staying less of a wager?

**Ruth**  
A radio that works. And somebody who comes for us if I'm wrong.

Hanne wrote a first-light fetch by the cutter across the foot of the sailing list, and a handset for the Calloways. Ruth read it twice and signed. Illuminara had asked for nothing she could not be refused.

The boat went out at half past six with a hundred and forty aboard, a bench on either side of the trunk, and a name the islanders had already given her: the Both. The second crossing left at half past twelve into rising swell, with Hanne's pencil never far from the line that said three. The third left at twenty past six in the evening with twenty-five people and a dog, into two point nine, and Illuminara sat on the trunk bench beside Tobi and did nothing but breathe when the stern lifted.

At ten to nine the last passenger stepped onto the shingle at Pellam Bank, into the headlights of the buses. A driver counted heads aloud, three hundred and five, and got the same number twice. Hanne's certificate, folded in her coat, carried two yard names on a single line.
On the bow ramp the two masters had not gone to the buses.

**Adaeze**  
Another fifty millimetres on the board and she'd hold the Sound like a church.

**Magnus**  
Another fifty and she'd dig on the bank like a spade.

They were still at it when the rain began, standing on the ramp with the shingle going dark around them, and neither moved off it. Behind them Illuminara put her blistered hands in her pockets, thought nothing wise, and listened. Far up the hill a lamp burned in the Calloway window, and on the hour Hanne's handset said, in Ruth's flat voice, *still here.*

accepted_lineage.note: Revision of T01 answering the three T02 priority points, all ACCEPTED. Kept: the question 'What did the sea do first?', the two deaths, the Marigold seven read as 267 versus 213 millimetres with no apology, Tobi's pin, Hanne's independence and abort thresholds, Illuminara's limited hold on the hull, the ugly boat, 305 carried and five staying, and the masters still arguing about fifty millimetres on the ramp. Changed: (P1) trunk physics corrected and the proof chain made checkable, nine-day build sequence with inspection gates, staged pin and bank tests; (P2) each master's proof condition, a cross-attack on one element, a costly concession and reciprocal signatures before ownership is divided; (P3) the Calloway refusal moved ahead of the trials and tied to a single exact rule with a coastguard owner, paid off in the last scene without claiming a rescue. Speaking roles unchanged at six (Adaeze, Hanne, Illuminara, Magnus, Ruth, Tobi); Wick stays silent. Outcome (3a): the same real result, now better earned: a tested, certified vessel carries 305 islanders in three loads, five remain safe under a bounded plan, and the two yards co-sign.

A case cracks. Then it's a hole with a lid on.

Adaeze stood at the rail with one hand flat on her chest and did not speak until the fifth wave had passed. Hanne read the compass off her board, wrote, and wrote again.

**Hanne**  
Eleven degrees at the worst, over five waves. Not fifteen. And I've seen what the board does not do, Adaeze. She still wants the rudder, and she still wants a helmsman who is awake. Both of those are in the boat.
Hanne laid the register on the wheelhouse table and put her finger on the line that mattered.

**Hanne**  
A hundred and forty seats on my certificate. Three hundred and ten names on the register. Five of those are the Calloways, standing by. They have a radio, high ground and a rule. The coastguard desk calls the house every hour from tomorrow noon. If the call is missed, or the gauge on Skerrow quay reads above four point two metres, the cutter goes up for them, and the desk owns that decision, not me. That leaves three hundred and five to carry. Two full crossings and a short third, each a little under six hours round trip. The sea builds through the last day. If the third has to wait for a window, it waits, and the cutter takes forty before it.

scenes.title: Three Crossings
paragraphs: *Tolland Slip to Pellam Bank · the day before the surge, 06:30*

The boat went out at half past six with a hundred and forty aboard, a bench on either side of the trunk, and a name the islanders had already given her: the Both. The second crossing left at half past twelve into rising swell, with Hanne's pencil never far from the line that said three. The third left at twenty past six in the evening with twenty-five people and a dog, into two point nine, and Illuminara sat on the trunk bench beside Tobi and did nothing but breathe when the stern lifted.

At ten to nine the last passenger stepped onto the shingle at Pellam Bank, into the headlights of the buses. A driver counted heads aloud, three hundred and five, and got the same number twice. Hanne's certificate, folded in her coat, carried two yard names on a single line.
On the bow ramp the two masters had not gone to the buses.

**Adaeze**  
Another fifty millimetres on the board and she'd hold the Sound like a church.

**Magnus**  
Another fifty and she'd dig on the bank like a spade.

They were still at it when the rain began, standing on the ramp with the shingle going dark around them, and neither moved off it. Behind them Illuminara put her blistered hands in her pockets, thought nothing wise, and listened. Far up the hill a lamp burned in the Calloway window. On the hour Hanne's handset said, in Ruth's flat voice, *still here,* and Hanne ticked it on her list. The gauge on Skerrow quay read three point one. The rule had not been touched, and it would be called again at nine.

accepted_lineage.note: Final after the T04 critique. Only P1 and P2 were addressed, both as bounded proof checks in scene 6, with the T03 text otherwise unchanged. Kept: 'What did the sea do first?', the two drownings, the Marigold seven as 267 versus 213 millimetres, reciprocal signed conditions, Tobi's pin, Hanne's independent abort power, Illuminara's limited and costly hold, the ugly boat, 305 carried and five staying by their own choice, and the unresolved fifty-millimetre argument on the ramp. Outcome (3a): a jointly designed, independently certified vessel carries 305 islanders in three loads through a building sea, five remain safe under a named rule, and the two yards keep their distinct knowledge and their argument; Illuminara's decisive contributions are the question that exposes two minutes of one crossing, the unit reading that turns 'seven' into two numbers, the demand that each master name what he must see, and fifty minutes holding a hull still.

story.title: THE LIFEBOAT TWO YARDS BUILT
story.deck: A surge is nine days off and the condemned ferry cannot sail. Two boatyards that have not shared a slip in thirty years each remember a drowning the other's boat would repeat; Illuminara asks them what the sea did first.
story.shape: Seven scenes across nine days: an argument on the shingle, a day in each yard, a chalk floor where one number turns out to be two and each master names what he would need to see, a night spent holding a hull still, a surveyor's gates and a trial in two seas with one family choosing to stay, and three crossings.

scenes.title: The Argument on the Shingle
paragraphs: *Skerrow, Tolland Slip · nine days before the surge, 06:40*

The ferry lay where the tide had left her, plating opened along one side like a tin. The surveyor's notice on her wheelhouse door was three days old. The forecast was newer: a surge in nine days, high water at 21:40, and a sea that would walk over the quay and into the lower village. Three hundred and ten people lived on Skerrow. The coastguard cutter could carry forty, if the sea allowed, and nobody would promise the sea.

Illuminara had come over on a fishing boat with a flask and a notebook. The council clerk had asked for hands that could hold a hull still while it was joined. Nobody had asked her for a design, and she was beginning to see why.
Two people had reached the slip from opposite ends of the shingle, and neither had slowed down.

**Magnus**  
There is a hull in my shed from the Orsay contract. Twenty-four metres, flat as a table, and she takes a bank like a hand takes a glove. I can have her on the slip by noon.

**Adaeze**  
And in the first following sea off the Sound she lies down. Flat doesn't grip. My brother learned that in the time it takes to say it. I won't send three hundred people out on a tray.

**Magnus**  
And your deep keel stands off Pellam Bank with nowhere to put its nose, and breaks up in the surf. My father learned that. Look at the stones.
Nobody looked at the stones. They looked at each other, the way people look at a wall they helped to build.

**Illuminara**  
I can hold a hull level while it is joined, and carry a load through it for a while. I can't draw a keel, and I can't draw a bank. Is each of you right about the other's boat?

**Adaeze**  
Yes.

**Magnus**  
Yes.

**Illuminara**  
Then I would like a day in each yard. Not to choose between you. To be corrected.
Magnus laughed first, short and unwilling. It was the first sound the two of them had made together in thirty years, and neither forgave the other for it.

scenes.title: The Loft
paragraphs: *Oyelaran yard, mould loft · nine days before the surge, 15:10*

Chalk lines covered the loft floor, every offset marked in Adaeze's fractions of a foot. A seventeen-year-old called Tobi had been told to teach the visitor to plane a keel timber and had decided to do it thoroughly.

**Tobi**  
Thumb forward. No, you're pushing the wood. The plane does the pushing. There. Hear that? That's a shaving, not a splinter.

Illuminara had stood inside a great many collapsing things and had never heard this sound. The oak smelled like a held breath. *I am being taught by a boy with sawdust in his eyebrows,* she thought, *and I am happier than I have been all week.*
Adaeze came up the stairs with two mugs and did not sit.

**Adaeze**  
Kehinde's boat was flat. A good boat, fast. Running home with the sea behind her, the stern came up on a wave and the bow dug, and for half a second she had nothing under her to hold the water. Then she swung beam-on, and the next wave finished it.

**Illuminara**  
What did the sea do first?

**Adaeze**  
The stern lifted. Everyone asks how big the wave was. You're the first to ask what it did first.
Illuminara wrote *stern lifts, no grip, swings beam-on* in her notebook, and under it, *open water, sea behind.* Adaeze watched her write it the way one watches a stranger handle a tool one has made.

**Adaeze**  
A keel is not a theory. It's the part of the boat that remembers the water.

scenes.title: The Bank
paragraphs: *Fenn yard, ramp and shingle · eight days before the surge, 07:20*

Wick, sixteen, put a chain in her hands and moved her grip before she had closed them. Everything on the Fenn ramp was measured in the yard's own rule, tenths of a foot, in pencil on the planking. Magnus walked the shingle beside her and told it to the stones rather than to her.

**Magnus**  
My father's boat had a good deep keel. Fine in the Sound. At Harbour Tarn there was no quay, only a bank like Pellam. He brought her in to ground her, and the keel took the shingle and stopped her dead while the surf kept coming. She lay down forty yards from dry stones.

**Illuminara**  
What did the sea do first?
He looked at her as if she had been impertinent. Then he answered.

**Magnus**  
The keel stopped. First. Then she turned over.

That night, on a sheet of the yard's brown paper, Illuminara wrote the two answers side by side. Adaeze's brother had died in open water, with the sea behind him and nothing to grip. Magnus's father had died on a bank, with the sea on the beam and too much to grip. *Two boats,* she thought. *Two different minutes of the same crossing.* Nobody had ever asked one hull to survive both.

scenes.title: Seven in Two Languages
paragraphs: *The old sail loft · seven days before the surge, 21:30*

Lamplight, and the two masters on opposite sides of it. Tobi and Wick stood against the wall with the look of apprentices who expect to be sent out. Illuminara had chalked two columns on the floor, every figure converted into millimetres. In one: OPEN WATER, SEA BEHIND. Needs grip along the length. In the other: THE BANK. Needs a flat bottom and nothing that can dig.

On the table lay a third sheet, brown at the folds, found at the bottom of the island's drawing chest. The Marigold, the one boat the two yards had ever drawn together, thirty years ago. Her keel was drawn at seven.

**Illuminara**  
Both your hands are on this sheet. What does seven mean?

**Adaeze**  
Seven-eighths of a foot.

**Magnus**  
Seven-tenths. It's what seven has always meant.

Seven-eighths of a foot is two hundred and sixty-seven millimetres. Seven-tenths is two hundred and thirteen. The Marigold had been built fifty-four millimetres too shallow, and she had rolled on her moorings the night she was launched, and for thirty years each yard had known exactly whose fault that was.
Nobody said sorry. Adaeze took the chalk and wrote 267 beside the seven. Magnus, after a long moment, took it from her and wrote 213 beneath it, and the two of them stood looking at the difference.

**Illuminara**  
Both are good drawings. You were reading one number in two languages.

**Magnus**  
Then show me a boat that does both, and I'll stop saying it can't be built.

**Adaeze**  
A board through the bottom. Down in the Sound, with the sea behind her, it gives her something to hold.

**Magnus**  
A hole in the bottom of a boat. That is near enough how my father went.

**Adaeze**  
The hole stays where it is, below the water. What changes is a case round it, welded up to the deck, so the sea rises inside the case to the level outside and no higher. The lid sits above her loaded waterline.

**Magnus**  
A case cracks. Then it's a hole with a lid on.

**Adaeze**  
Then it is filled with water and watched all night before she moves. And hear what the board is. It is grip along her length and nothing else. It does not steer her and it is not ballast. She still wants her rudder, her weight in the right place and someone on the helm who knows a following sea.

**Magnus**  
And on the bank the board is down and she stops dead, the way he did.

**Tobi**  
Raise it before she lands. And if she meets shingle with the board half down it should kick up, not dig. A pin that shears. A winch to haul it, and a crank for when the winch won't.
Nobody answered an apprentice for a while. Adaeze looked at Magnus. Magnus looked at Wick, who looked at the floor, and then, with some effort, at Tobi.

**Illuminara**  
I can't tell you whether it will work. I can ask what each of you would have to see before the other's hand is on your work.

**Adaeze**  
In a two-and-a-half-metre sea from astern, board down, she holds her heading within fifteen degrees for five waves running. Measured with the surveyor's compass, not remembered. Otherwise Kehinde's boat sails again with my name on it.

**Magnus**  
Nothing under her bottom when she touches shingle. The board housed by pin or by crank inside twenty seconds, and I watch her take the bank twice, once slow and once not. Otherwise it's my father's boat under three hundred people.
Then each of them did the thing the other had been waiting thirty years for, and attacked the drawing instead of the man.

**Magnus**  
Your board is drawn for the deep Sound. A hundred and fifty millimetres off its depth, and the pin shears at a load I can watch it shear at.

**Adaeze**  
A hundred and fifty is grip I would rather keep.

**Magnus**  
Then it digs.

**Adaeze**  
And your stern is cut square. A following sea sits on a square stern like a hand on a table. I want it faired before I trust the board to hold her.
Neither spoke for a time. The lamp ticked. Outside, the tide went out over the stones.

**Adaeze**  
Then the board is shorter. And you cut your Orsay hull.

**Magnus**  
Nobody has cut an Orsay hull. I'd cut it myself, in my own shed, and you check my frames in your units.

**Adaeze**  
And I fair the stern to your drawing, in your tenths.

On the brown sheet, under Tobi's pin, Adaeze wrote Magnus's condition and signed it, and Magnus wrote hers and signed it, each figure in feet or tenths and again in millimetres. Neither of them looked up while they did it.

**Magnus**  
Who owns what?

**Adaeze**  
Board, case and pivot are mine. Hull, ramp and the framing around the slot are yours.

**Magnus**  
I check your pivot load in your units.

**Adaeze**  
And I check your frames in yours. Then we both do it again in millimetres and sign each other's sheets.

**Illuminara**  
I'll hold her still while you cut.

scenes.title: Standing Still
paragraphs: *Tolland Slip, shed two · four days before the surge, 02:10*

Three days had gone into the hull, in the order Hanne Voss's sheet laid down. On the first, the Fenn yard stripped the deck and brought the Orsay hull to the slip. On the second, Oyelaran's plate shop rolled the case and the two yards framed round the slot line in alternating shifts, so that neither slept while the other's hands were on the boat. On the third, Hanne walked every frame with a torch, rejected two welds, and passed the rest at midnight and not before. Only then was the bottom to be cut.
She sat on her blocks now with a seam of lamplight where the slot would go. Fourteen tonnes of plating wanted to spring the moment Tobi's saw finished the first cut; a flat hull opens badly.

Illuminara laid both palms against the plating beside the line and took the load through herself, down her arms and her spine into the slip, the way one holds a door against wind. The plating stayed true. For fifty minutes Magnus cut and Tobi cut and Adaeze measured, and she did not move.

It cost her. Her hands shook long before the slot was done, and when Magnus said, without looking up, that she might let go, she sat down on an upturned bucket and could not lift a mug. Tobi brought her tea and, with a straight face, a plane.

**Tobi**  
Your grip is still wrong.
*Good,* she thought, and was surprised again by how much she meant it.

scenes.title: Two Seas
paragraphs: *Skerrow hill, Pellam Bank and Skerrow Sound · two days before the surge, 06:00*

Ruth Calloway's family did not come to the slip. Illuminara went up the hill instead and found Ruth on her step with a flask. Five of them lived in that house, and the church where her mother lay was thirty-four metres above the sea.

**Ruth**  
I've lived through eleven forecasts. We are staying.

**Illuminara**  
What would make staying less of a wager?

**Ruth**  
A radio that works. And somebody who comes for us if I'm wrong.

**Illuminara**  
I'll take that to the surveyor. If she can't make it hold, I'll come back and tell you so.

Between the cut and the water there had been two days. The case was welded, filled to the lid and watched through a night, and it held. The hoist and the crank were fitted. On the slip, Tobi's pin sheared under the rig at the load he had set, and sheared at the same load the second time. She went down the slip at first light, ugly, with the trunk running down her middle like a spine.
Hanne Voss was sixty and had refused certificates for far prettier boats. She read her conditions aloud before anyone touched the engine.

**Hanne**  
Abort thresholds first. Heel past fifteen degrees and holding, I call her in. A board that doesn't answer a command inside twenty seconds, I call her in. Water at the trunk lid, I call her in. Sea above three metres significant, I call her in. I will not be argued with, by either yard or by you.

She went through the boat before the bank, and she let both masters watch her do it. She put a torch down the trunk, ran a hand along the seams of the case, tried the pivot for play, read the freeboard against the ballast, and worked the hoist and then the crank herself, with a watch in her other hand. Seventeen seconds on the crank. She wrote it down.

At Pellam Bank, on the rising tide, the boat went at the shingle at two knots with the board housed. Her flat bottom rode up the bank and stopped without a shudder. Then, on Hanne's order, again at two knots with the board dropped halfway. It struck, the pin sheared, and the board swung up into its trunk like a hand taken off a hot stove. Hanne went below with her torch before anyone spoke. She found a crushed pin stub, a pivot that was true and seams that were dry. Tobi fitted a fresh pin in four minutes. They did it again at four knots, and Hanne went below again. Magnus watched the whole of it with his arms folded.

**Magnus**  
Good pin.
In his mouth it was a speech.

In the Sound that afternoon the swell ran two and a half metres from astern, and she went out carrying a hundred and forty people's weight in water ballast, the tanks gauged to the tonne, because Hanne would not certify a boat that had only ever been tried light. The boat lifted her stern on the first wave with the board down, and she did not swing. Adaeze stood at the rail with one hand flat on her chest and did not speak until the fifth wave had passed. Hanne did not call her in at five. She kept her on the heading for forty minutes, well over two hundred waves, and read the compass off her board, and wrote, and wrote again. Then she brought her back to the slip and went below with the torch before she would put her name to anything. The trunk lid was dry. The seams were dry. The pivot was true.

**Hanne**  
Eleven degrees at the worst, and that was the worst of forty minutes, not just of five waves. Not fifteen. Loaded to a hundred and forty, and the trunk and the pivot clean after it. And I've seen what the board does not do, Adaeze. She still wants the rudder, and she still wants a helmsman who is awake. Both of those are in the boat.
Hanne laid the register on the wheelhouse table and put her finger on the line that mattered.

**Hanne**  
A hundred and forty seats on my certificate. Three hundred and ten names on the register. Five of those are the Calloways, standing by. They have a radio, high ground and a rule. The coastguard desk calls the house every hour from tomorrow noon. If the call is missed, or the gauge on Skerrow quay reads above four point two metres, the cutter leaves harbour for the quay and asks them again at the door. It can work that quay safely up to five metres and not above, so four point two is when it goes, not when it is too late. The desk owns that decision, not me. That leaves three hundred and five to carry. Two full crossings and a short third, each a little under six hours round trip. The sea builds through the last day. If the third has to wait for a window, it waits, and the cutter takes its twenty-five, with room for the five besides.

The second crossing left at half past twelve into rising swell, with Hanne's pencil never far from the line that said three. The third left at twenty past six in the evening with twenty-five people and a dog, into two point nine, and Illuminara sat on the trunk bench beside Tobi and did nothing but breathe when the stern lifted.

At ten to nine the last passenger stepped onto the shingle at Pellam Bank, into the headlights of the buses. A driver counted heads aloud, three hundred and five, and got the same number twice. Hanne's certificate, folded in her coat, carried two yard names on a single line.
On the bow ramp the two masters had not gone to the buses.

**Adaeze**  
Another fifty millimetres on the board and she'd hold the Sound like a church.

**Magnus**  
Another fifty and she'd dig on the bank like a spade.

The rule had not been touched, and it would be called again at nine.
